title: The Tenth Guru's book
hook: compiled after his death, traditionally by Bhai Mani Singh; its make-up is discussed respectfully among Sikhs

segments.voice: Yesterday the Gurus' teachings closed, from the second Guru through the fifth, and the ninth. Your line was one teaching, many voices. Which voice did you choose to return to? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-two.

Some books are finished by their authors. Others are finished by the people who loved them. A teacher dies, and a student goes from house to house, collecting copies of what was written, sorting them, setting them in order. The book that comes out of it is treasured. And because the teacher didn't set the order himself, readers can ask, gently, which page came from which hand. A new block of the path starts today, the writings of Guru Gobind Singh, and it starts with a book like that.
screen: `FINISHED BY THOSE WHO LOVED HIM.` → `COPIES GATHERED, SET IN ORDER.` → `WHICH PAGE, WHICH HAND?`

segments.voice: Its name is Dasam Granth: the book of the Tenth. It holds writings associated with Guru Gobind Singh. Tradition says it was compiled after his death, and it names Bhai Mani Singh, a learned Sikh of the Guru's circle, as the one who gathered it. So this book was not set in order by the Guru himself the way the Adi Granth was set in order by Guru Arjan. That difference matters, and Sikhs keep it in view. Here is what sits inside. Some of it Sikhs pray every day: Jaap Sahib, and verses from Akal Ustat, are among the morning prayers of the Sikh daily round, and tradition places some of its prayers at the Khalsa initiation. There is Bachitar Natak, a poem that tells parts of his own story. There is the Zafarnama, a letter in Persian. And there are long retellings of old Indian tales that read very differently from the hymns. Now the honest part. The Guru Granth Sahib is the Guru for Sikhs; the Dasam Granth is not. And Sikhs discuss which parts of the Dasam Granth come from the Guru's own pen. Some hold that all of it does. Some hold that the prayers clearly do and other parts may come from poets in his court. At its best, that discussion keeps a careful tone, because it's about a beloved teacher's words. Nobody on this path will be told which side to take. For the next weeks, we'll read the parts Sikhs pray and quote, and say so plainly when a question is open.
screen: `THE BOOK OF THE TENTH.` · `GATHERED AFTER HIS DEATH.` · `PRAYERS, A LIFE, A LETTER.` · `NOT THE GURU; ITS MAKE-UP DISCUSSED.` · then, large: `DISCUSSED WITH RESPECT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read about its history, the way a careful reader would. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one question you hold where honest people land in different places. A family question, a work question, a question of faith. Notice how you speak about the people who see it the other way. Try one sentence about them that they would recognize as fair. Then, later today, read one short account of how the Dasam Granth was gathered, and notice its tone as much as its facts. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Dasam Granth. The book of the Tenth: writings of Guru Gobind Singh gathered after his death, with daily prayers inside, and a make-up Sikhs discuss with care. Today's word.
Your line: discussed with respect. Today, when a disagreement comes up, describe the other side in words they would sign. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite Jaap Sahib and verses from Akal Ustat, both found in the Dasam Granth, among their daily prayers; the Guru Granth Sahib alone is installed and honored as the Guru.

fork.setup: a beloved teacher has died, and a student has gathered his writings. readers disagree about who wrote one page. what do they do?
options: keep reading, and keep asking with care.
